title: Argus Analytics - Discovery: migration from OpenAI to Dedicated
summary: Discovery call for Argus Analytics evaluating migration from OpenAI hosted usage to Redwood Dedicated (and exploring Private). Key drivers: cost predictability, latency consistency, and data control for PII-sensitive workloads. Discussed eval parity (model outputs), compatibility with current vLLM/TGI pipelines, benchmarking approach, security requirements (SOC 2, SSO, KMS), and a pilot plan. Next steps: share pricing, security docs, and benchmark template; run a two-week pilot with throughput/latency targets.
topics: dedicated vs hosted vs private tradeoffs
action_items: Maya Chen: Share Redwood Dedicated pricing sheet and pilot agreement by 2026-07-16
Diego Ramos: Send benchmark template (benchmark-template.xlsx) and suggested test prompts by 2026-07-17
Sofia Martin / Argus: Provide sample eval prompt set and 3 typical workloads by 2026-07-20
Noah Kim / Argus: Send SOC2 report request list and KMS key rotation policy questions by 2026-07-16
next_steps: Redwood to send pricing + pilot contract
Schedule in-region benchmark run (Diego to coordinate with Sofia)
Security doc share: SOC2, ISO summary, encryption/KMS notes
Follow-up meeting to review pilot results and SLOs in ~3 weeks
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. We're joined by Diego on the technical side. Quick intros?
[00:10] Liam Patel: Liam Patel, CTO at Argus Analytics. We build extraction pipelines and a search+RAG layer on top of customer docs.
[00:20] Sofia Martin: Sofia, ML engineer, I own model infra and evals.
[00:25] Noah Kim: Noah, security. I'll cover compliance questions.
[00:30] Maya Chen: Great — quick agenda, understand current infra, goals for migration, constraints, and next steps. Diego, do you want to kick off on compatibility?
[00:40] Diego Ramos: Sure. So Argus mentioned you're currently using OpenAI for generation and embeddings, and running some local inference with vLLM/TGI for on-prem tests. Is that right?
[00:50] Sofia Martin: Yeah, that's right. We have most traffic hitting OpenAI via API, about 1.2 million tokens/day, spikes up to 250 QPS for short prompts. For specialized workloads we spin up vLLM locally with TGI for cost reasons, but it's been rough — memory mgmt and KF cache, um kv cache, I mean, is tricky.
[01:10] Diego Ramos: Got it. A lot of customers have that hybrid pattern. What's the main pain with OpenAI? Cost unpredictability or latency?
[01:18] Liam Patel: Both. Cost is spiky with heavy QPS. Latency variance affects our SLA. Also data residency — some customers require data not leave region.
[01:27] Maya Chen: OK. So you're evaluating Redwood Dedicated to get reserved capacity and also reduce variance, plus possibly Redwood Private for data residency?
[01:34] Liam Patel: Exactly. We want predictable unit economics and to keep PII on-prem for some accounts. Also need compatibility so our current prompts and evals produce same-ish outputs — eval parity.
[01:44] Diego Ramos: For eval parity, we usually run a side-by-side with a small eval set to compare outputs, BLEU/ROUGE or embedding distance, and qualitative checks. Do you have a gold prompt set?
[01:54] Sofia Martin: We have about 300 prompts and 50 longer transcripts used for quality gates. Can share.
[02:00] Diego Ramos: Perfect, that's good for a pilot. A couple technical notes: Redwood Dedicated supports the main open models you mentioned, and the runtime has optimizations similar to vLLM — continuous batching, KV cache management, and quantization options. The TGI/vLLM pipelines typically need adapter work for some kernels; we usually run a compatibility shim for your existing clients.
[02:18] Sofia Martin: When you say quantization options, do you mean we can run 4-bit on dedicated nodes? We care about quality drop.
[02:25] Diego Ramos: Yes, we have supported quant profiles tested for each model family. We recommend running evals with 8-bit int8 and a 4-bit QAT variant to see quality vs cost. Often 4-bit is fine for many generative tasks but we should validate on your prompt set.
[02:36] Noah Kim: On the security front, two things: KMS integrations and audit logs. We need to ensure customer keys can be used — HSM/KMS — and that logs are retained for 12 months. Also SSO/SAML is required.
[02:48] Maya Chen: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and on-prem control plane; Dedicated can integrate with BYOK in many cases. We do SOC 2 and can provide the report. We also emit detailed per-request audit logs — you can configure retention.
[03:00] Liam Patel: Good. How about model compatibility: our devs are used to OpenAI API semantics and also some custom headers for routing. Will we need to rewrite a lot of code?
[03:10] Diego Ramos: We expose a compatible REST API and SDKs; most teams can swap endpoints with minimal changes. For internal vLLM/TGI infra, we can provide an adapter that keeps your existing client code intact and handles streaming differences. There may be small differences in streaming chunk sizes but nothing major.
[03:25] Sofia Martin: Streaming and function-calling parity matter for us — we rely on streaming tokens for real-time UIs.
[03:30] Diego Ramos: We support streaming and function/tool calling. For function calling we validate the structured outputs. We'll include those tests in the pilot.
[03:36] Liam Patel: What about throughput and latency numbers? We ran some basic benchmarks on vLLM but it doesn't scale predictably.
[03:44] Diego Ramos: For Dedicated, we size GPU pools based on your peak QPS and sequence length distribution. For example, a 4xA100 pool with autoscaling gave X sustained QPS for 4096-context for a model family — we can share specific benchmarks. The key is batching behavior; if your workload is lots of short prompts, we'll configure small-aggregation windows to keep latency low.
[04:05] Maya Chen: We have a public perf sheet but I'll attach a tuned baseline for Argus-like workloads.
[04:11] Liam Patel: Pricing — how does reserved capacity compare to our current OpenAI spend?
[04:17] Maya Chen: Typically dedicated reserved capacity reduces per-token cost significantly at your scale, and gives predictable monthly commit. I'll send a modeled comparison based on your reported 1.2M tokens/day.
[04:28] Noah Kim: For compliance, we need answers on data retention, reproduction of logs for audits, who has access to keys. Also if Redwood personnel can access customer data in Dedicated/private setups.
[04:40] Maya Chen: For Dedicated, customer data is isolated; access is restricted and audited. For Private deployments, you control the control plane. We'll send the SOC2 and the security whitepaper; Diego will include architecture notes for KMS/BYOK.
[04:52] Sofia Martin: On migration effort — how long is an expected pilot? We don't want a months-long ramp.
[04:58] Diego Ramos: Typical pilot is 2–4 weeks: baseline eval, benchmark runs, and a small production shadow to validate SLOs. We can do a two-week quick pilot focusing on eval parity and latency/throughput targets.
[05:10] Liam Patel: Sounds good. One more: model versions. We lock to a pinned model for stability?
[05:15] Maya Chen: Yes, customers pin model versions; we also support staged rollouts/canaries. You'll be able to pin and then roll forward after validation.
[05:23] Sofia Martin: About vLLM/TGI differences — we've observed different sampling randomness across runtimes which changes outputs. How do you ensure parity?
[05:31] Diego Ramos: We recommend deterministic seeds for sampling tests and run multiple seeds to measure variance, plus embedding distance metrics for semantic parity. For generation, we'll run manual QA on 50 samples to confirm acceptability.
[05:42] Liam Patel: Competitive question — are you seeing migration from Anthropic or other vendors differently?
[05:47] Maya Chen: Many customers migrate from Anthropic/OpenAI for cost or control; differences are mostly around API semantics and model behavior, but our tooling focuses on making parity testing easy.
[05:55] Noah Kim: Legal/procurement — we'll need terms and a security addendum. Can you share a sample contract?
[05:59] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll include a sample pilot agreement.
[06:03] Priya Rao: Who is the day-to-day contact for the pilot?
[06:06] Maya Chen: Diego will own the technical pilot and coordinate with Sofia. I'll manage the commercial side.
[06:10] Diego Ramos: I'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and a short runbook for how we'll execute tests, including scripts to reproduce vLLM/TGI runs.
[06:18] Sofia Martin: Great — please include instructions for seeding and sample prompt set.
[06:22] Diego Ramos: Will do.
[06:24] Liam Patel: Recap then — Redwood to send pricing and pilot contract, Diego to send benchmark template and runbook, Argus to share prompt/eval set and compliance questions. We'll aim to start pilot next week.
[06:36] Maya Chen: Yep. Anything else?
[06:38] Noah Kim: No, that's it. Thanks.
[06:40] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone.
[06:43] <end of recording>

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words (e.g., "KV cache" sometimes transcribed as "KF cache"). Speaker labels mostly accurate though there are short overlaps.

References/Artifacts mentioned: pricing model doc (link: https://redwood.ai/docs/dedicated-pricing), security whitepaper (link: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2), benchmark-template.xlsx (shared by Redwood), redwood-hosted-vs-dedicated.pdf (attached in follow-up).
